Part 1: Everything Glows
:::

*Thermal radiation*

---

## Thermal Radiation {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
All objects with temperature above **absolute zero** emit electromagnetic radiation.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is **thermal radiation** — comes from thermal motion of particles.

No external source needed — the object emits because it has internal energy.
:::

::: {.notes}
3–4 min. "Even you, at ~310 K, emit ~100 W of infrared light."
:::

---

## Examples Across Temperatures {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Object | Temperature | Peak Wavelength | Emission |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|----------|
| Cosmic background | 2.7 K | ~1 mm | Microwaves |
| Room temperature | 300 K | ~10 μm | Infrared |
| Red-hot metal | ~1000 K | ~3 μm | Near-IR, dull red |
| Sun's surface | 5800 K | ~500 nm | Visible (green peak) |
| Hot blue star | 30,000 K | ~100 nm | Ultraviolet |

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
**Pattern:** Hotter → shorter wavelength
:::

::: {.notes}
4–5 min. "Cool objects emit infrared. Hot objects emit visible and UV."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Thermal Radiation {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Which of the following emits thermal radiation?

- [ ] Only the Sun and stars
- [ ] Only objects that are visibly glowing
- [x] Everything with temperature above absolute zero
- [ ] Only objects connected to power sources
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## What Is a Blackbody? {background-color="black"}

A **blackbody** is an idealized object with two properties:

::: {.incremental}
1. It **absorbs all incident radiation** — nothing reflected
2. It emits thermal radiation with a spectrum determined **only by temperature**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Temperature alone determines the spectrum.

A blackbody iron ball at 5800 K emits the same spectrum as a blackbody tungsten ball at 5800 K — or the Sun.
:::

::: {.notes}
5–6 min. "The spectrum is universal — depends only on T."
:::

---

## The Blackbody Spectrum {background-color="black"}

{{< fig blackbody-spectrum-temps >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
- Hotter → peak shifts to shorter wavelengths (bluer)
- Hotter → curve is taller (more total energy)
:::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. "Two effects: peak shifts AND total energy increases."
:::

---

## Why Stars Are (Nearly) Blackbodies {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.incremental}
1. Stars are **opaque** — photons interact many times before escaping
2. Those interactions **thermalize** the radiation
3. The light we see comes from the **photosphere** — characterized by temperature
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Real stellar spectra have **spectral lines** on top of the blackbody continuum.

We'll use those lines in Lecture 9 for composition and motion.
:::

::: {.notes}
7–8 min. "Stars approximate blackbodies for the smooth continuum."
:::

---

- [x] Only the object's temperature
- [ ] The type of EM wave hitting it
:::

1 min. iClicker poll.

A) Doubles
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
B) Stays the same
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}

30 sec. Have students vote before revealing.

## Wien's Displacement Law {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2,900,000 \text{ nm}}{T \text{ (K)}}$$

**Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is the astronomer's thermometer:

Measure peak wavelength → know the temperature.
:::

::: {.notes}
8–9 min. "Wien's Law lets us measure stellar temperatures remotely."
:::

---

## Wien's Law in Action {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Object | Temperature | Peak Wavelength | Where |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|-------|
| Cool red star | 3000 K | ~970 nm | Near-infrared |
| Sun | 5800 K | ~500 nm | Green visible |
| Hot white star | 10,000 K | ~290 nm | Ultraviolet |
| Hot blue star | 25,000 K | ~120 nm | Far ultraviolet |

::: {.notes}
9–10 min. "Hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths."
:::

---

## Worked Example

**Problem:** A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm (UV). What is its temperature?

::: {.fragment}
$$T = \frac{2,900,000 \text{ nm}}{290 \text{ nm}} = 10,000 \text{ K}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is a hot, blue-white star — about 1.7× the Sun's temperature.
:::

::: {.notes}
10–11 min. Walk through the calculation.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Wien's Law {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
A cool red star has a surface temperature of 3000 K. Where does its spectrum peak?

- [ ] 100 nm (ultraviolet)
- [ ] 500 nm (visible green)
- [x] 970 nm (near-infrared)
- [ ] 10,000 nm (far infrared)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Solution:** $\lambda = 2,900,000/3000 = 967$ nm ≈ 970 nm (near-IR).
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## The "Sun Is Green" Puzzle {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
Plug in the Sun's temperature (5800 K):

$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2,900,000}{5800} = 500 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
That's **green light!**

Yet the Sun doesn't look green...
:::

::: {.notes}
11–12 min. "So why doesn't the Sun look green?"
:::

---

## Why the Sun Isn't Green {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**1. Blackbody curves are broad.**

The Sun emits across ALL visible wavelengths — not just the peak.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**2. Our eyes see the mix as white.**

When all colors are present, we perceive white light.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
If the Sun emitted ONLY at 500 nm, it would look green.

But blackbody spectra are continuous and broad.
:::

::: {.notes}
12–13 min. "Broad spectrum → white appearance."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Why Not Green? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
The Sun's blackbody spectrum peaks at ~500 nm (green). Why doesn't the Sun appear green?

- [ ] The Sun doesn't actually emit green light
- [ ] Earth's atmosphere absorbs all the green
- [x] The Sun emits broadly across all visible wavelengths; we see white
- [ ] Our eyes can't see green light
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

| Color | Temperature | Example Stars |
|-------|-------------|---------------|
| Red/orange | 3000–4500 K | Betelgeuse, Antares |
| Yellow | 5000–6000 K | Sun, Alpha Centauri A |
| White | 7000–10,000 K | Sirius A, Vega |
| Blue-white | 10,000–30,000+ K | Rigel, Spica |

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
**Wien's Law in action: color reveals temperature.**
:::

::: {.notes}
13–14 min. "No thermometer needed — just analyze the color."
:::

## Predict First! {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
If you **double** an object's temperature, its total energy output...
:::

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="25%"}
A) Doubles
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
B) Quadruples
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
C) ×8
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**D) ×16** ✓
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
30 sec. Have students vote before revealing.
:::

---

## Stefan-Boltzmann Law {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$\text{Power per area} = \sigma T^4$$

**Temperature has a HUGE effect on luminosity.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
$\sigma$ is the **Stefan–Boltzmann constant** (a fixed constant). Use $T$ in **Kelvin**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The **fourth power** is dramatic:

| Temperature Factor | Luminosity Factor |
|-------------------|-------------------|
| 2× hotter | $2^4 = 16×$ more luminous |
| 3× hotter | $3^4 = 81×$ more luminous |
| 10× hotter | $10^4 = 10,000×$ more luminous |
:::

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. "Temperature is the dominant factor in stellar luminosity."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Stefan-Boltzmann {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Star A has twice the surface temperature of Star B. If both have the same radius, Star A is:

- [ ] 2× more luminous
- [ ] 4× more luminous
- [ ] 8× more luminous
- [x] 16× more luminous
:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

---

## The L-T-R Connection {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$$

**Luminosity depends on both size (R²) and temperature (T⁴).**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
Here, $L$ is total power output (luminosity), $R$ is radius, and $T$ is the star’s effective surface temperature (K). This uses the **blackbody approximation**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
A star can be luminous because:

- It's very **hot** (even if small)
- It's very **large** (even if cool)
- Or both!
:::

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. "This is how we distinguish giants from dwarfs."
:::

---

## Same Temperature, Different Luminosity {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center}
Two stars at the **same temperature** but **different luminosities**...

must have **different sizes**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
If Star A and Star B have the same $T$ but Star A is 100× more luminous...

Then Star A has **10× the radius** (since $L \propto R^2$).
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
This is how we distinguish **giants** from **dwarfs**.
:::

::: {.notes}
16–17 min. "Same color, different brightness → different size."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig betelgeuse-size-eso >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
**Betelgeuse** is a red giant — same color as red dwarfs, but ~1000× the radius.
:::

::: {.notes}
17–18 min. "Same temperature, vastly different size."
:::

---

## Worked Example

**Problem:** Two stars have the same temperature. Star A has 100× the luminosity of Star B. How do their radii compare?

::: {.fragment}
Since $L \propto R^2 T^4$ and $T$ is the same:

$$\frac{R_A}{R_B} = \sqrt{\frac{L_A}{L_B}} = \sqrt{100} = 10$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Star A has **10× the radius** of Star B.
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. Walk through the calculation.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Giants vs Dwarfs {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
A red giant and a red dwarf have the same surface temperature. The giant is 10,000× more luminous. How do their radii compare?

- [ ] Giant's radius is 10× the dwarf's
- [x] Giant's radius is 100× the dwarf's
- [ ] Giant's radius is 10,000× the dwarf's
- [ ] Their radii are the same
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Solution:** $R_{giant}/R_{dwarf} = \sqrt{10,000} = 100$.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## Quick Check: L-T-R Synthesis {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Star X is twice as hot as Star Y and has half the radius. How does Star X's luminosity compare?

- [ ] Same luminosity
- [ ] 2× more luminous
- [x] 4× more luminous
- [ ] 8× more luminous
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Solution:** $L_X/L_Y = (1/2)^2 \times (2)^4 = 1/4 \times 16 = 4$.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm}

1. **Everything above absolute zero emits thermal radiation.** Hotter → more and at shorter wavelengths.

2. **Blackbody** spectrum depends only on temperature.

3. **Wien's Law:** $\lambda_{peak} = 2,900,000/T$ (nm, K). Hot → blue. Cool → red.

4. **The Sun peaks at green** but appears white because it emits broadly.

5. **Stefan-Boltzmann:** Power per area $\propto T^4$. Doubling $T$ → 16× more luminous.

6. **L-T-R:** $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$. Same temperature, different luminosity → different size.

7. **Blackbodies reveal temperature, but not composition.** For that, we need spectral lines (L9).

:::

::: {.notes}
19–21 min. Rapid recap.
:::

## {.center background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Numerical Verification
:::

*Checking Wien and Stefan-Boltzmann with real stars*

::: {.notes}
Let's verify our equations with explicit calculations.
:::

---

## Wien's Law: The Sun {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:** Sun's surface temperature $T = 5778$ K

$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^6 \text{ nm·K}}{T}$$

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^6 \text{ nm·K}}{5778 \text{ K}} = 501.5 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Unit check:** $\frac{\text{nm·K}}{\text{K}} = \text{nm}$ ✓
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .bg-muted .p-2}
**501 nm is green light!** Yet the Sun appears white because:

1. Blackbody curves are broad (emits all visible colors)
2. Our eyes see the mix as white
:::

::: {.notes}
"I'm using the more precise Wien constant 2.898×10⁶ nm·K. The rounded 2.9×10⁶ gives 502 nm."
:::

---

## Wien's Law: Betelgeuse {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:** Betelgeuse surface temperature $T \approx 3500$ K

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^6 \text{ nm·K}}{3500 \text{ K}} = 828 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**828 nm is in the near-infrared!**

Betelgeuse's peak is *beyond* visible light.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Why does it look red?**

The visible portion of its spectrum is dominated by red wavelengths (the "tail" of the blackbody curve in the visible range).
:::

::: {.notes}
"Cool stars peak in the infrared. We see the red edge of their emission."
:::

---

## Wien's Law: Rigel {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:** Rigel surface temperature $T \approx 12,000$ K

::: {.fragment}
$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^6 \text{ nm·K}}{12,000 \text{ K}} = 241.5 \text{ nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**241 nm is ultraviolet!**

Rigel's peak is *shorter* than visible light.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Why does it look blue-white?**

The visible portion of its spectrum has more blue than red (we see the "rising edge" toward the UV peak).
:::

::: {.notes}
"Hot stars peak in UV. We see the blue-dominated tail in the visible."
:::

---

## Summary: Peak Wavelength vs. Appearance {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Star | T (K) | λ_peak (nm) | Peak Location | Visible Color |
|------|-------|-------------|---------------|---------------|
| Betelgeuse | 3,500 | 828 | Near-IR | Red |
| Sun | 5,778 | 502 | Green | White |
| Sirius A | 9,940 | 292 | UV | Blue-white |
| Rigel | 12,000 | 242 | UV | Blue |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Pattern:** We never see a "green star" because:

- Cool stars peak in IR → red visible tail
- Hot stars peak in UV → blue visible tail
- In between → roughly equal visible colors → white
:::

::: {.notes}
"The blackbody curve shape prevents green stars from existing."
:::

---

## Stefan-Boltzmann: The Sun's Luminosity {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Calculate the Sun's total power output.**

::: {.fragment}
**Given:**

- Stefan-Boltzmann constant: $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴)
- Sun's temperature: $T = 5778$ K
- Sun's radius: $R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^8$ m
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Formula:**

$$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"Let's compute this step by step with careful units."
:::

---

## Sun's Luminosity: Step by Step {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Step 1: Surface area**

$$A = 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi (6.96 \times 10^8 \text{ m})^2 = 6.08 \times 10^{18} \text{ m}^2$$

::: {.fragment}
**Step 2: T⁴ calculation**

$$T^4 = (5778 \text{ K})^4 = 1.115 \times 10^{15} \text{ K}^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Step 3: Combine**

$$L = (6.08 \times 10^{18} \text{ m}^2) \times (5.67 \times 10^{-8} \frac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{K}^4}) \times (1.115 \times 10^{15} \text{ K}^4)$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"Let's track units carefully through this calculation."
:::

---

## Sun's Luminosity: Unit Analysis {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

$$L = [\text{m}^2] \times \left[\frac{\text{W}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{K}^4}\right] \times [\text{K}^4]$$

::: {.fragment}
The m² cancels:

$$L = \left[\frac{\text{W} \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{K}^4}\right] \times [\text{K}^4] = [\text{W}] \quad \checkmark$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Numerical result:**

$$L = 6.08 \times 10^{18} \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 1.115 \times 10^{15}$$

$$L = 3.84 \times 10^{26} \text{ W}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**The Sun outputs 3.84 × 10²⁶ watts** = 384 trillion trillion watts!
:::

::: {.notes}
"This matches the measured solar luminosity. Stefan-Boltzmann works!"
:::

---

## How Many Light Bulbs? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

The Sun's luminosity: $L_\odot = 3.84 \times 10^{26}$ W

A typical LED bulb: 10 W

::: {.fragment}
**Number of bulbs to match the Sun:**

$$N = \frac{3.84 \times 10^{26} \text{ W}}{10 \text{ W}} = 3.84 \times 10^{25} \text{ bulbs}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
That's **38 trillion trillion** LED bulbs!

Or about 5 billion bulbs for every human who has ever lived.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Just to give you a sense of scale. The Sun is absurdly powerful."
:::

---

## L-T-R Verification: Comparing Stars {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Problem:** Sirius A is 25× more luminous than the Sun and has $T = 9940$ K. What's its radius?

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{L_{\text{Sirius}}}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{R_{\text{Sirius}}}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T_{\text{Sirius}}}{T_\odot}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$25 = \left(\frac{R_{\text{Sirius}}}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{9940}{5778}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$25 = \left(\frac{R_{\text{Sirius}}}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times (1.72)^4 = \left(\frac{R_{\text{Sirius}}}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times 8.76$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{R_{\text{Sirius}}}{R_\odot} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{8.76}} = \sqrt{2.85} = 1.69$$
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**Sirius A is 1.7× the Sun's radius.**
:::

::: {.notes}
"Sirius is hot (so more luminous per area) and slightly larger."
:::

---

## {.center background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Deeper Dive
:::

*The ultraviolet catastrophe and quantum mechanics*

::: {.notes}
Optional advanced content on the history of blackbody radiation.
:::

---

## The Ultraviolet Catastrophe {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**The problem (circa 1900):**

Classical physics predicted that a hot object should emit **infinite energy** at short wavelengths!

::: {.fragment}
Classical prediction (Rayleigh-Jeans):

$$B(\lambda) \propto \frac{T}{\lambda^4}$$

As $\lambda \to 0$, energy $\to \infty$. Obviously wrong!
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .bg-warning-subtle .p-2}
This was called the **"ultraviolet catastrophe"** — classical physics broke down.
:::

::: {.notes}
"This was a crisis. The best physics of the time predicted nonsense."
:::

---

## Planck's Quantum Solution (1900) {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Max Planck's radical idea:**

Energy isn't continuous — it comes in discrete packets: **quanta**.

$$E = nhf$$

where $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...$ (integers only!)

::: {.fragment}
**Why this fixes the catastrophe:**

At short wavelengths, $hf$ is large.

Creating even ONE quantum requires lots of energy.

At finite temperature, high-energy quanta are exponentially suppressed.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Planck didn't fully believe his own solution at first. But it worked."
:::

---

## The Planck Function {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**The correct blackbody spectrum:**

$$B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \times \frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_B T} - 1}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Key features:**

- At long wavelengths: reduces to classical Rayleigh-Jeans
- At short wavelengths: exponentially suppressed (no catastrophe!)
- Peak wavelength: Wien's Law emerges naturally
- Total power: Stefan-Boltzmann emerges naturally
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
Wien's Law and Stefan-Boltzmann are **consequences** of the Planck function, not independent laws!
:::

::: {.notes}
"This equation contains all of blackbody physics. Everything we learned follows from it."
:::

---

## Birth of Quantum Mechanics {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

Planck's solution (1900) required $E = hf$.

::: {.fragment}
**Einstein (1905)** showed light itself comes in quanta: **photons**.

**Bohr (1913)** showed atoms have quantized energy levels.

**Heisenberg & Schrödinger (1925-26)** developed full quantum mechanics.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-muted .p-2}
**The blackbody problem launched the quantum revolution!**

Planck's constant $h$ appears everywhere in modern physics.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Trying to understand why hot things glow the way they do led to quantum mechanics."
:::

---

## Why Stars Are Nearly Perfect Blackbodies {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Three conditions for blackbody radiation:**

::: {.incremental}
1. **Thermal equilibrium:** Radiation and matter have exchanged energy enough times to reach the same temperature.

2. **Opacity:** Photons scatter many times before escaping (information about source is "forgotten").

3. **Temperature determines spectrum:** Only T matters, not composition.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Stars satisfy all three:** Dense stellar interiors thermalize radiation over thousands of years before it escapes from the photosphere.
:::

::: {.notes}
"The interior of the Sun is a 15-million-degree blackbody. We see the cooler 5800 K photosphere."
:::
